problem: Learned embodied visual navigation policies assume the agent's action space is identical at training and test time, so they break when the action space changes (e.g. different step sizes or turn angles). Few methods address this mismatch.
motivation: In real deployment, the robot's action space often differs from the one used for training, and retraining from scratch for each new action space is costly. A policy that stays robust to action-space changes and adapts with few samples would make navigation policies more transferable.
key_idea: Use a two-stage adversarial learning framework: stage one learns an action-space-robust representation of the agent's state, and stage two adapts the policy to a new action space with few samples.
insight: Only the abstract was available, so no ablations can be cited. The abstract implies that an adversarially learned, action-space-invariant state representation is what enables transfer to new action spaces with fewer training samples.
method: Action-insensitive navigation task: defines a new problem in which the training and testing action spaces of the agent differ.
Stage 1 adversarial training: a robust adversary learning framework learns a feature representation of the agent's states that is robust to the action space.
Stage 2 adaptation training: transfers the trained policy to new action spaces using fewer training samples.
